instructions:
Read the paper below and produce a structured summary.

It matched these tracked topics; `relevance` must contain one entry per slug, stating what this paper changes for that topic:
- overthinking: Overthinking — When and why large reasoning models think more than a problem needs (or less than it needs) — the accuracy/efficiency tradeoff of reasoning length, test-time compute scaling, and methods to make a model stop, or keep going, at the right point.

Answer `models` explicitly, even when the answer is `[]`. List the checkpoints the work trains, evaluates or analyses, named as the paper names them — a base model, a released model, a judge. A paper that evaluates none returns an empty list, and that is a real answer: the archive holds several. Leaving it out looks identical to that in the record, and nothing afterwards can tell the two apart.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

concepts: string - reusable ideas this paper relies on or introduces
datasets: string - datasets, benchmarks, corpora or simulators used. Not models: a checkpoint that was evaluated or fine-tuned belongs in `models`.
output_schema.limitations: string - stated limits plus any the reader should notice
output_schema.method: string - how it works, enough for a reader to explain it
methods: string - named methods, architectures or algorithms
models: string - models the work trains, evaluates or analyses, as named in the paper (e.g. a base checkpoint, a released reasoning model, a judge)
output_schema.one_liner: string - what the paper does, in one sentence, no hype
output_schema.problem: string - the problem it addresses and why it is open

relevance.<topic-slug>: string - why this matters for that specific topic

output_schema.results: string - headline numbers, on which benchmarks, against what

payload.title: Smaller, Weaker, Yet Better: Training LLM Reasoners via Compute-Optimal Sampling

contributions: a systematic compute-matched comparison of stronger-expensive vs. weaker-cheap language models as sources of synthetic reasoning training data
characterization of the coverage/diversity/false-positive tradeoff between weak and strong data sources
a novel weak-to-strong training paradigm, alongside knowledge distillation and self-improvement, all showing weaker-cheaper data outperforms stronger-costlier data at fixed compute
result.limitations: Not stated in the fetched abstract beyond the three training paradigms and compute-matched comparison methodology described.
result.method: Compares data sampled from a stronger-but-more-expensive (SE) model against data sampled from a weaker-but-cheaper (WC) model under matched compute/inference budgets (so the WC model can generate proportionally more samples for the same cost), measuring coverage, diversity, and false-positive-rate of the resulting training data, then evaluating downstream reasoner performance across three training paradigms: knowledge distillation (training a separate smaller student), self-improvement (a model trained on its own generations), and a proposed weak-to-strong improvement paradigm (a stronger model trained on data generated by a weaker one).
result.one_liner: Under a fixed inference budget, training data generated by a weaker-but-cheaper (WC) language model consistently produces better-performing reasoner students than data from a stronger-but-more-expensive (SE) model, across knowledge distillation, self-improvement, and a novel weak-to-strong learning paradigm -- challenging the default practice of sourcing synthetic training data from the most powerful available model.
result.problem: Synthetic training data for LLM reasoners is conventionally sourced from the strongest available models under the assumption that higher-quality generations are worth their higher cost, but it was untested whether this is actually compute-optimal once a fixed total inference/sampling budget is held constant across the comparison.

relevance.overthinking: Indirectly relevant: this is about training-data source selection (which model generates the SFT/RL data) rather than inference-time reasoning length, but it is a compute-optimal-under-fixed-budget result of the same flavor as several overthinking-mitigation papers in this archive -- more inference compute spent one way (many cheap weak-model samples) can outperform less compute spent expensively (fewer strong-model samples), paralleling the archive's broader theme that where compute is spent matters more than how much is spent.

result.results: WC-generated data shows higher coverage and diversity than SE-generated data at matched compute budgets, at the cost of a higher rate of false-positive (incorrect but superficially plausible) solutions. Despite this higher error rate, models trained on WC-generated data consistently outperform those trained on SE-generated data across all three paradigms tested (knowledge distillation, self-improvement, and weak-to-strong improvement) at a fixed sampling/inference budget.
